title: Different timescales for generalized attraction and category-specific repulsion in numerosity perception
abstract: The sense of number is a fundamental ability supported by dedicated neural mechanisms. Because natural scenes often contain multiple object groups, numerosity may be encoded in a category-specific manner. Consistent with this idea, adaptation effects are reduced when adaptor and test stimuli differ in category, particularly when category signals object identity (e.g., color but not motion). We asked whether this category-selectivity extends to other stimulus-history effects. Integrating past information into current perception may support the formation of discrete object representations from continuous input. Accordingly, both session-level (central tendency) and trial-level (serial dependence) biases may be category-tuned. We tested this hypothesis by manipulating color and motion features, each defining categories mapped to distinct numerosity ranges, presented either in blocked or interleaved sessions. Overall, we observed a comparable pattern across color and motion. At the session level, blocked presentations revealed a perceptual effect opposite to the compression predicted by range-specific central tendency. Interleaving abolished this effect and promoted convergence toward a prior shared across categories. At the trial level, the interleaved presentation provided both category repetitions and alternations, allowing us to examine how history effects unfold as a function of temporal lag and category match. We observed a characteristic temporal profile, with short-lag attraction, intermediate neutrality, and long-lag repulsion. Notably, attraction was category-independent, whereas repulsion was selectively observed for category repetitions. Overall, these findings show that multiple stimulus-history effects shape numerosity perception depending on the temporal and categorical structure of the environment, with category-selectivity primarily emerging in the repulsive bias.
